title: SIEM Forwarder & Emergency Approval Proxy — PRD (draft)
summary: This PRD outlines a lightweight on-prem 'Redwood Forwarder' for customers to forward compact, tamper-evident audit slices into their SIEMs, plus an 'Emergency Approval Proxy' component that enables time-bounded operator actions with stricter dual-approval workflows. The goal is to meet enterprise evidence and incident workflows for Private deployments while minimizing customer integration work and protecting PII/keys.
goals: Deliver a small-footprint agent customers can run in their VPC or on-prem to export audit events to their SIEM (syslog/HTTP/S3) in a compact, schema-driven format.

Provide an emergency approval proxy that mediates ad-hoc critical operations (e.g., emergency rollback, operator override) and records dual-approval artifacts into both Redwood audit ledger and customer SIEM.
Ensure exported data is tamper-evident, privacy-preserving (PII minimization), and integrates with common SIEM mappings out-of-the-box (Splunk/Elastic/QRadar).
Keep operational burden low: support streaming and batched export, backpressure handling, and predictable cost/retention profiles for exported artifacts.
non_goals: Not building a full SIEM connector ecosystem (no native app for each SIEM). We'll provide canonical formats and examples for Splunk/Elastic/QRadar and a simple syslog/http/azure/s3 sink.
Not storing customer PII on Redwood side — forwarder should perform masking/aggregation before export by default.
Not replacing customer's existing incident response playbooks; we aim to augment them with additional evidence streams and a standardized emergency approval artifact.
requirements: Functional: agent can export events in two modes: streaming (TLS) and batch (periodic compressed uploads to S3-compatible endpoints).
Functional: each export batch includes a compact manifest with event count, time window, SHA256 root hash, and an incremental HMAC chain for integrity verification.

Functional: approval proxy exposes an API that requires two distinct operator signatures (can be same org but different principal) before executing an emergency action; proxy emits a signed approval artifact to both Redwood's control-plane (if connected) and the local forwarder audit stream.
Non-functional: agent <200MB memory typical, single-core friendly; must run on small customer VMs/containers.
NFR: end-to-end export latency SLA: streaming under 5s to SIEM (network-dependent), batch uploads configurable (default 5m).
Security: mutual TLS or mTLS where supported; support X.509 client certs and API key fallback for on-prem sinks.
Privacy: configurable redaction rules prior to export (regex-based and schema-aware), default redaction config applied for PII types (emails, SSNs, keys).
Interoperability: include mapping templates for at least Splunk Event Collector (HEC), Elastic ingest pipeline (beats/Logstash), and RFC5424 syslog.
data_format: Proposal: newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON), each line = compact event envelope. Mandatory envelope fields: event_id, timestamp (ISO8601), event_type, source (redwood-forwarder), minimal_payload (JSON string or base64 if binary), redaction_level (NONE/REDACTED/AGGREGATED), prev_hmac (hex). Batch manifest is a small JSON file with {batch_id, start_ts, end_ts, count, root_hash, batch_hmac, compressed_size_bytes}. Integrity: forwarder uses an HMAC-SHA256 chain where each event HMAC = HMAC(secret, prev_hmac || event_line). The manifest HMAC commits to root_hash and batch metadata. Customers can verify using the shared verification key or public verification endpoint. We include an optional 'compact-proof' header for quick integrity checks (8-byte prefix).
approval_flow: Primary flow: operator A requests emergency action via Redwood Console or local API; action is marked 'pending'. Operator B receives a notification and must digitally sign/approve within time window (configurable, default 15 minutes). Approval Proxy verifies both principals (OAuth SSO or X.509) then issues an 'approval token' signed with proxy's private key. Token is recorded as an event by the forwarder and sent to customer SIEM. If the control plane is reachable, token is additionally posted to Redwood's control-plane audit ledger. Execution only proceeds after token recorded. Emergency bypass: for jurisdictional needs we support a time-limited single-approver bypass only when an external 'pager-duty' heartbeat confirms on-call escalation AND an encrypted out-of-band HSM-signed recovery token is presented — this is intentionally cumbersome and logged as a high-severity event. All approvals include metadata: approver_id, approver_group, justification text, action_id, timewindow, and verifier_signature.
security_privacy: Agent stores minimal keys: ephemeral enrollment token and per-customer verification key. Long-lived secrets must be in customer KMS (optional integration).
Default behavior: redact values matching PII patterns and replace with deterministic placeholders (hash truncated) to enable correlation without exposing raw PII.
Forwarder supports running with reduced privileges and can be deployed as non-root container.
operational_considerations: Backpressure: streaming sink errors must be retried with exponential backoff; if prolonged failures occur, agent switches to local batching and raises an operator alert.
Retention and tiering: manifest retains index metadata locally for 30 days (configurable); customers should configure SIEM retention according to compliance needs.
Observable metrics: per-sink throughput, pending-batches, last-successful-hmac, approval-token-latency. Provide Prometheus metrics and a lightweight health HTTP endpoint.
Upgrade story: agent supports rolling upgrades and schema versioning; manifest includes schema_version. Older control-plane connectors must reject future-incompatible schema.
compliance_and_forensics: Design for forensic replay: batch manifests + compact-proof allow reconstructing a contiguous event stream for a given time range. For high-assurance customers, we offer an optional WORM S3-compatible sink recipe and a signed archival manifest (time-stamped by customer's HSM or Redwood co-signed timestamp).
open_questions: What is the minimum acceptable proof primitive for customers that cannot share HMAC keys with Redwood (we propose a public verification endpoint or offline key exchange).
Should the approval proxy require hardware-backed keys for both approvers in the default config? (Pros: stronger non-repudiation; Cons: setup complexity).
What list of SIEM field mappings will cover >75% of customer needs out-of-the-box? We should run a short survey with 10 customers.
Edge case: network partition where control-plane is unreachable — do we allow local-only approvals that never reach Redwood control-plane? If yes, how to surface trust boundaries to product teams?
out_of_scope: Deep native integrations and apps for each SIEM vendor, long-term cold storage on Redwood side, or building a customer SIEM troubleshooting UI inside Redwood Console. We will provide artifacts and examples, not full managed SIEM connectors.
risks: Customer misconfiguration could lead to leaking redacted fields — must be mitigated with conservative default redaction and a pre-flight validator.
Approval proxy becomes a single point of failure if deployed centrally — default recommendation is customer-run proxy inside VPC with optional Redwood co-hosted availability for hybrid customers.
Operational complexity for customers with strict air-gapped environments; we must provide clear offline installation and verification docs.
next_steps: Engineering spike (2w): build a minimal forwarder that emits NDJSON with HMAC chain to local file and a syslog sink.
Security review (1w): threat model for approval proxy and key lifecycle; decide on default HSM requirement.
Customer discovery (2w): interview 8 customers (mix of enterprise and regulated) for SIEM mapping and emergency workflow needs.
Prototype demo: create a Splunk HEC ingest example, Elastic ingest pipeline, and an RFC5424 syslog sample, then run end-to-end verification with one pilot customer.
notes_to_self: Keep this PRD focused on pragmatic deliverables. Avoid big-bang features. Prioritize privacy-by-default, low-friction onboarding, and clear optics for any 'bypass' paths.
authors_commentary: Drafted in product-private-deployments + security. This doc mixes product and operational design; expect iterations after the engineering spike and the security threat model review.
